transcript.text: We replaced our old condenser dryer with a heat pump one about a month ago and honestly it's driving me mad, a normal load of towels takes nearly 3 and a half hours, the old one did it in about 90 minutes. It also feels barely warm for the first half hour when I open the door to check. Surely that's not right? Is it faulty?

It may well be normal rather than a fault. Heat-pump dryers deliberately run much cooler than an old condenser dryer and take considerably longer; a towel load taking around 3½ hours can be within normal expectations. Feeling only mildly warm during the first half-hour is also not, by itself, a fault. Before judging it faulty:
1. With the dryer switched off, clean the door lint filter and any lower heat-pump/foam filters exactly as the manual describes. Restricted airflow is the commonest reason for unnecessarily long cycles.
2. Use a normal Cotton/Towels programme with the intended dryness level, rather than Eco/low-heat/iron-dry if those are selected. Keep the drum no more than roughly two-thirds full.
3. Make sure the towels have had the washer's highest suitable spin first; towels that go in very wet can add a lot of drying time. The key test is the result at the end: if the towels are properly dry after the full cycle, the cooler, slower operation is probably just the trade-off of a heat-pump dryer. If they remain damp after a full cycle with clean filters and a normal well-spun load, that is not normal and the dryer should be checked under its warranty—initially for airflow/sensor issues, and then the heat-pump system if needed.

Right, well I clean the fluff filters after every load and I did the other filter two weeks ago, it looks clean. It's the Cotton Cupboard Dry programme with a full drum, and the towels come out of the washer at 1000 rpm. They do come out fully dry in the end, just takes forever. Is that still normal?

Yes — on the information so far, that still sounds likely to be normal heat-pump behaviour rather than a fault. The strongest reassurance is that the towels are fully dry at the end: a heat-pump dryer runs much cooler and can take far longer than an older condenser dryer. A full drum of absorbent towels, spun at 1000 rpm, is close to a worst-case load for drying time, so around 3½ hours is plausible. It is not a like-for-like comparison with the old, hotter condenser dryer. The useful comparison is one reduced, better-spun load:
1. Fill the drum only to around two-thirds with towels.
2. Use the washer’s highest spin that is suitable for those towels.
3. Run the same Cotton Cupboard Dry programme. If that is noticeably quicker and still dries fully, there is no sign of a dryer fault — it is the normal capacity/energy-saving trade-off of a heat-pump machine. If a reduced, well-spun load still takes exceptionally long, or performance worsens and laundry starts finishing damp, then it would be worth raising under warranty for an airflow, sensor or heat-pump-system check.

Ok, I can try a smaller load. Does it matter that the dryer lives in my garage? It's pretty cold out there at the moment, and I do open the door a couple of times during the cycle to check how it's getting on.

Yes, both can matter. A heat-pump dryer in a cold garage can take longer because it has less warmth available to recover and circulate. Check the installation section of its manual for the permitted room-temperature range; if the garage is below that range, slow drying is expected and performance can become poor in very cold weather. Opening the door also adds time. Each time, the dryer loses its warm air and takes in cold, damp garage air; it then has to rebuild the conditions needed to dry. The drum feeling only mildly warm is still normal for a heat-pump machine. The most likely explanation remains normal heat-pump behaviour, compounded by a full load of towels, a 1000 rpm spin, cold surroundings and the door being opened. The fact the towels finish fully dry argues against a failed heat-pump circuit or sensor. For the useful comparison, run the smaller, better-spun towel load without opening the door until it ends. If it is appreciably quicker, there is no meaningful fault indication. If it remains very slow even with that test, and the garage is within the manual’s stated temperature range, raise it with the retailer/manufacturer while it is under warranty.
I don't know what temperature range the manual says, I'd have to dig it out. The garage is about 8-10 C at the moment and I can't move the dryer indoors. Will that be why it's so slow then?

Yes — 8–10°C is very likely a significant reason it is slow. Heat-pump dryers recover heat from the surrounding air, and that is much harder in a cold garage. Combined with a full drum of heavy towels, a 1000 rpm spin and opening the door during the cycle, a 3½-hour Cotton Cupboard Dry cycle can be normal, especially when the towels are fully dry at the end. It does not prove there is a fault. In fact, finishing properly dry makes a failed heat-pump system or sensor much less likely. The mildly warm drum is also normal for this type of dryer; it will not feel like the old hotter condenser dryer. The best separating test is one smaller towel load: fill the drum to about two-thirds, use the highest suitable washer spin, and leave the door shut until the programme ends. If it is noticeably quicker and dries fully, the garage temperature and load conditions are the explanation. If that test is still taking an exceptionally long time, check the manual or manufacturer support page for its minimum operating temperature. Many heat-pump dryers have a stated ambient-temperature range, and 8–10°C may be near or below the recommended lower limit depending on the make. If the garage is within its specified range and the reduced test remains very slow, use the warranty to have the airflow, temperature sensing and sealed heat-pump system assessed.

candidates: Normal lower-temperature, longer heat-pump drying cycle (high)
Restricted airflow from lint or heat-pump filters (medium)
Load, spin speed or programme selection increasing drying time (medium)
